imageCaption: The Gomez family's luggage arranged by the apartment door at dawn, the butterfly container catching the first light, a framed photo of Riverside Park balanced on top of the largest suitcase.
text:
The apartment was wrong.

Aaliyah realized this at 5:47 AM while standing in the kitchen holding a glass of water she didn't remember pouring. The light coming through the window was the wrong color—too blue, too filtered, like it was traveling through something that shouldn't be there. And the apartment itself had that quality of somewhere that was already becoming a memory, even though they were still inside it.

They weren't supposed to leave until 8:15 AM. The flight was booked for 10:40. But something about the morning felt accelerated, like the timeline was gently pushing them toward the door.

"You're awake," Luisana said. She appeared in the doorway with her journal and a cup of coffee that definitely hadn't been there five minutes ago. "I've been awake since four. Couldn't sleep. Every time I closed my eyes, I kept thinking about the fountain. How it was making music yesterday, and today we're leaving it to make music for people we won't see again."

Aaliyah didn't respond immediately. She was looking at her mother's hands—one holding the coffee, one holding the journal, both of them slightly trembling. Not from cold. From the specific shakiness that comes from endings, even the good ones.

"We taught them how to resonate," Aaliyah said finally. "The neighborhood. They don't need us to keep the frequency going. That was literally the point. We showed up, we created the pattern, we left so they could learn to hold it."

"I know that logically," Luisana said. She sat down at the kitchen table—the small one where they'd eaten breakfast for the past ten days, which now seemed impossibly temporary. "But logic and feelings are having a disagreement this morning."

Elijah appeared from the bedroom already wearing his travel hoodie, the one with the collection of patches he'd been adding to throughout the trip. Most of them were stickers from places they'd visited, but one was from yesterday—a paper one that Marco had made, featuring a terrible drawing of the fountain and the words "Riverside Park Official Glitch Inspector" in marker.

"Sully threw up," Elijah announced. He said this with the specific matter-of-factness of someone reporting weather. "On my backpack. I think he's nervous about flying. Or he's expressing solidarity with my emotions. Sully does that sometimes—he throws up when people he loves are having complicated feelings."

"That's not a thing," Aaliyah said automatically.

"It's definitely a thing," Elijah countered. "He did it the morning Mom was worried about leaving her job. And the day Dad couldn't decide whether to book tickets to Argentina. He throws up. It's his way of saying 'I understand that we're in a transition and I am also processing.'"

Anthony appeared in the doorway with Sully in his arms—the dog looking vaguely guilty but also deeply committed to being carried. There was a small pile of paper towels visible in the background of the bedroom.

"He's going to be fine," Anthony said, addressing the room's collective anxiety. "Sully's thrown up on every form of transportation we've ever used. It's his ritual. It means he's ready for the next thing. Right, buddy?"

Sully licked Anthony's face with the enthusiasm of someone who'd just vomited and was now ready to move on to more important matters.

"The taxi's coming in an hour," Luisana said. She was checking her phone, which had that specific notification-heavy look of a family that was about to do something. "I confirmed it this morning. And Marco's going to meet us at the airport—he wants to photograph us leaving."

"Of course he does," Elijah said. He pulled out a chair and sat down with the specific grace of someone who'd decided to officially treat this as a Real Moment requiring his presence. "This is the part of the story where the family leaves the neighborhood that saved them. Marco would document his own appendix surgery if it had a good narrative arc."

There was a noise from the living room—a soft, distinctive sound of something being moved. Anthony's head jerked up.

"No," he said. He set Sully down gently and headed toward the living room. "Tell me you didn't."

Aaliyah followed, Luisana and Elijah close behind. What they found was Marco, standing over the suitcases, holding Anthony's license plate collection—the pegboard that had been carefully rolled in protective paper and scheduled for luggage intake.

Except the paper was gone. And the pegboard wasn't rolled up. It was mounted on the wall.

"What are you doing?" Anthony said. Not angry. Just confused in the way of someone who'd planned a specific thing and was watching someone else make different plans.

"You'll roll it back up at the airport," Marco said. He didn't turn around, just kept adjusting the mounting. The collection caught the wrong-colored morning light and threw it back in fragments—every territory they'd visited was suddenly visible, suddenly glowing. "But first, I'm photographing it. Not for documentation. For here. For this apartment that you're leaving."

Anthony stared at him. "You're leaving the collection on the wall."

"You're leaving it on the wall," Marco corrected. He finally stepped back to admire the mounting. The pegboard looked permanent now, official, like it belonged to this apartment more than it belonged to the suitcases. "When the next family moves in, they'll find it. Or maybe the landlord will take it down. But for a few days, or a few weeks, or maybe longer—there will be a map hanging here. A record of everyone you went and why you went. And whoever lives here next will have to decide what to do with it."

"That's not the plan," Anthony said. But he was walking closer to the collection, studying it with an expression Aaliyah couldn't quite read. "The plan was to take it to Curaçao."

"Plans change," Marco said gently. "Especially for your family. And I'm thinking—you've been collecting places this whole journey. But you've been leaving places too. You've been leaving marks. Riverside Park has the resonance frequency. The neighborhood has the pattern. And this apartment is going to have the proof that you were here, that you traveled, that you made it beautiful."

Elijah appeared at Aaliyah's shoulder. He was studying the collection with the specific intensity of someone who was about to say something that sounded simple but would turn out to be profound.

"The collection's a map of where we've been," Elijah said slowly. "But a map is just a tool to help you remember that there are other places. You don't need to carry the map to Curaçao if you already know where Curaçao is. You already know because you've been learning all along."

Anthony looked at his youngest son. Then at the collection. Then at Marco, who was adjusting the mounting one final time, making sure it would stay when the family left.

"We're not taking the collection," Anthony said. It wasn't a question.

"You're not," Marco confirmed. "But you're leaving it. Which is different. You're leaving proof. You're saying 'we were here, and it mattered, and someone should know.'"

Luisana made a sound—not quite a laugh, not quite a sob, something in between. She was holding her journal open to yesterday's entry, and Aaliyah could see the words: "Sometimes the best maps are the ones we leave behind."

"We need to take this down before the taxi comes," Anthony said finally. His voice was doing that thing where it got thick. "We need to pack it properly."

"We need to leave it," Luisana said. She was walking toward her husband with the specific certainty of someone who understood what the collection had actually been all along. "Marco's right. We've been carrying proof of everywhere we've been. But the real mark we left was in the people, in the neighborhood, in the frequency that's still making music at Riverside Park. The plates can stay."

"But Abuela Ida—" Anthony started.

"Would tell you," Luisana interrupted gently, "that home isn't a collection of places. It's the willingness to leave them behind and trust that the moment you learned there is enough."

Sully, sensing a moment of profound family understanding, walked over and lay his head on Anthony's foot with the precision of a dog offering both comfort and agreement.

Aaliyah watched her father looking at the mounted collection one final time. She watched him release it—not physically, but in every other way that mattered. She watched him turn toward the door, toward the taxi, toward Curaçao and whatever came next.

"One picture," Marco said. He was already raising his camera. "All of you. In front of the collection. Leaving it behind."

The family gathered. They stood in front of the mounted pegboard with the wrong-colored light hitting them sideways, and Marco captured the moment—the goodbye that looked like moving forward, the collection that looked like staying.

When they left the apartment seventeen minutes later, the license plate was still on the wall. Glowing softly in the morning that felt like it belonged to multiple times at once.

Tomorrow, Curaçao. But today, they were learning the difference between carrying a map and trusting you've already learned the route.

The taxi was waiting. The door closed behind them. And somewhere in the apartment, in that room with the mounted collection, the blue morpho butterfly—the one they'd left behind on the kitchen table, next to the empty coffee cup—began to move its wings.

Ready for whatever came next.
